definition: The occurrence of fortunate discoveries by chance, especially while looking for something else.
example: Finding my favourite bookshop was pure serendipity — I was only looking for shelter from the rain.
etymology: Coined by the English writer Horace Walpole in 1754, after a Persian fairy tale, "The Three Princes of Serendip", whose heroes kept making discoveries they were not seeking. Serendip is an old name for Sri Lanka.
fact: Walpole invented the word in a letter to his friend Horace Mann. It stayed obscure for nearly two centuries before becoming a favourite of scientists describing lucky discoveries.

definition: A fixed amount of money paid to an employee, usually expressed per year and paid monthly.
example: She took a lower salary in exchange for a four-day week.
etymology: From Latin salarium, derived from sal, "salt". The original sense was probably an allowance connected with salt, perhaps money for buying it.
fact: The popular story that Roman soldiers were paid in salt has no solid ancient evidence behind it — but the link between salarium and sal is real.

definition: A band of fibrous tissue in the body that contracts to produce movement.
example: Climbing works muscles you didn't know you had.
etymology: From Latin musculus, "little mouse", a diminutive of mus. A flexing muscle was thought to look like a mouse moving under the skin.
fact: Greek made the same comparison: μῦς (mŷs) means both "mouse" and "muscle". The shellfish "mussel" comes from the same Latin word.

definition: A sudden event, such as an accident or natural catastrophe, that causes great damage or loss.
example: The first rehearsal was a disaster, but opening night went perfectly.
etymology: Via French désastre from Italian disastro, from dis- (expressing something bad) + astro, "star". A disaster was literally an ill-starred event, blamed on an unfavourable position of the planets.
fact: Shakespeare plays on the astrological sense in King Lear, where Edmund mocks people who blame their disasters on the sun, the moon and the stars.

definition: A person or animal with whom one spends a lot of time or with whom one travels.
example: The dog was his constant companion on long walks.
etymology: From Old French compaignon, from Late Latin companio, literally "one who shares bread with another": com- ("with") + panis ("bread"). It may be a loan-translation of a Germanic word with the same structure.
fact: "Company" shares the same bread-sharing origin, so every company is, etymologically, a group of people who eat together.

definition: A period of isolation imposed on people, animals or goods that may carry an infectious disease.
example: The new arrivals spent two weeks in quarantine.
etymology: From Italian (Venetian) quaranta giorni, "forty days" — the period ships arriving from plague-stricken ports had to wait before passengers and cargo could land.
fact: The first recorded rule of this kind, from Ragusa (today's Dubrovnik) in 1377, required only thirty days; forty became the standard later.

definition: The deliberate destruction, damage or obstruction of something, especially for political or military advantage.
example: Investigators ruled out sabotage and blamed a faulty valve.
etymology: From French saboter, "to bungle, botch" (originally "to clatter, knock about"), from sabot, a wooden clog.
fact: The tale that striking workers threw their clogs into machines is a colourful folk etymology. The word more likely comes from the idea of working clumsily, as if stomping about in clogs.

definition: A sentimental longing or wistful affection for a period in the past.
example: The smell of chalk filled him with nostalgia for his school days.
etymology: Coined in 1688 by the Swiss medical student Johannes Hofer from Greek nóstos ("homecoming") + álgos ("pain"), as a learned translation of the Swiss German word Heimweh, "homesickness".
fact: Nostalgia began as a medical diagnosis — a supposedly dangerous illness of Swiss mercenaries serving far from home. Its sense of longing for a past time rather than a place came much later.

related.note: nostalgia was coined to translate it

definition: A piece of evidence or information that helps solve a problem or mystery.
example: The muddy footprint was the first real clue.
etymology: A respelling of clew, "a ball of thread or yarn", from Old English cliwen.
fact: The sense comes from Greek myth: Theseus escaped the Minotaur's labyrinth by following a ball of thread (a clew) given to him by Ariadne. Following a clue still means following the thread to a way out.

definition: A machine capable of carrying out a complex series of actions automatically.
example: A robot now does the welding on that line.
etymology: From Czech robot, coined from robota, "forced labour, drudgery", for Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots).
fact: Karel Čapek credited his brother, the painter Josef Čapek, with suggesting the word. Karel's own first idea was "labori".

definition: A pear-shaped fruit with leathery skin, smooth buttery flesh and a large stone.
example: Mash the avocado with lime and a pinch of salt.
etymology: From Spanish avocado, an alteration of aguacate (from Nahuatl āhuacatl) under the influence of avocado, an old Spanish form of abogado, "lawyer".
fact: French went the same way: avocat means both "avocado" and "lawyer".

definition: A school or class that prepares children, usually aged four to six, for primary school.
example: Our youngest starts kindergarten in September.
etymology: Borrowed from German Kindergarten, "children's garden", the name the educator Friedrich Fröbel gave in 1840 to his school in Bad Blankenburg.
fact: Fröbel imagined children as plants that grow best when tended like a garden. He also designed educational toys called "Fröbel gifts".

definition: A colourless volatile liquid (ethanol) produced by fermentation; also drinks containing it.
example: The dish is cooked long enough for the alcohol to evaporate.
etymology: Via Medieval Latin from Arabic al-kuḥl, "the kohl" — a fine powder used as eye make-up. Alchemists extended it to any finely refined substance, then to the "essence" or spirit obtained by distillation.
fact: So alcohol is, in a roundabout way, the same word as kohl eyeliner.

definition: A deep, long-lasting, often pensive sadness with no obvious cause.
example: There was a gentle melancholy to the empty seaside town in winter.
etymology: From Greek melankholía, "black bile": mélas ("black") + kholḗ ("bile").
fact: Ancient and medieval medicine held that health depended on four humours — blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. Too much black bile was thought to cause gloom.

definition: To exclude someone from a society or group.
example: He was ostracized by colleagues after reporting the fraud.
etymology: From Greek ostrakízein, from óstrakon, "potsherd" — a broken piece of pottery.
fact: In 5th-century BC Athens, citizens could vote to exile a politician for ten years by scratching his name on a potsherd. Thousands of these ballots have been dug up by archaeologists.

definition: Free from pretence or deceit; proceeding from genuine feelings.
example: Please accept my sincere apologies.
etymology: From Latin sincerus, "clean, pure, sound", of uncertain further origin.
fact: You may hear that sincere comes from sine cera, "without wax", supposedly praising sculptures that had no cracks filled with wax. It's a myth — a popular folk etymology with no ancient support.

definition: Details, considerations or pieces of information of little importance or value.
example: Her head is full of film trivia.
etymology: From Latin trivia, the plural of trivium, "place where three roads meet" (tri- + via). Things heard at a crossroads were common, everyday talk.
fact: In medieval universities the trivium — grammar, logic and rhetoric — made up the three basic liberal arts, which is part of why "trivial" came to mean elementary or unimportant.

definition: A danger or risk; something that could cause harm.
example: Loose cables are a trip hazard.
etymology: From Old French hasart, the name of a game of chance played with dice, possibly from Arabic az-zahr, "the die".
fact: Hazard was a popular dice game in medieval England and an ancestor of the casino game craps.

gloss: opening in a wall for light
definition: An opening in a wall or vehicle, usually fitted with glass, that lets in light or air.
example: Leave the window open a crack.
etymology: From Old Norse vindauga, literally "wind-eye": vindr ("wind") + auga ("eye").
fact: Before the Viking-age borrowing took over, Old English used eagþyrel, "eye-hole". Spanish ventana is also built on a word for wind, Latin ventus.

gloss: to throw out of a window
definition: To throw someone or something out of a window; informally, to remove someone from power.
example: Frustrated, she threatened to defenestrate the printer.
etymology: From Latin de- ("down from") + fenestra ("window").
fact: The word is closely tied to Prague: in 1618 Protestant nobles threw two Catholic regents and their secretary out of a castle window. All three survived, and the event helped trigger the Thirty Years' War.

definition: Used to express good wishes when parting.
example: We said goodbye at the station.
etymology: A contraction of "God be with ye", recorded from the late 16th century. "God" was later replaced by "good" on the model of greetings like "good day" and "good night".
fact: Early spellings include "godbwye" and "god buy'ye". Many farewells work this way — Spanish adiós and French adieu both mean "to God".

definition: Declared in law to be unable to pay outstanding debts.
example: The airline went bankrupt after a single bad winter.
etymology: From Italian banca rotta, "broken bench". Banca was the bench or counter at which a moneylender did business.
fact: It is traditionally said that a failed banker's bench was broken to show he could no longer trade. Whether or not that was the custom, the Latin rupt- ("broken") was swapped in under the influence of words like "rupture".

gloss: lingering at the table after a meal
definition: The time spent relaxing and talking around the table after a meal has finished.
example: La sobremesa duró más que la comida.
exampleTranslation: The after-lunch chat lasted longer than the meal itself.
etymology: From sobre ("over, on top of") + mesa ("table").
fact: There's no single-word English equivalent. In Spain a weekend sobremesa can easily last a couple of hours.

definition: The early hours of the morning, from after midnight until dawn.
example: Llegamos a casa a las tres de la madrugada.
exampleTranslation: We got home at three in the morning.
etymology: From madrugar ("to get up early"), from Vulgar Latin *maturicare, based on Latin maturus, "early, timely, ripe".
fact: A popular proverb: "A quien madruga, Dios le ayuda" — God helps those who get up early, Spanish for "the early bird catches the worm".

definition: Pregnant. (Not "embarrassed" — that's avergonzada.)
example: Mi hermana está embarazada de seis meses.
exampleTranslation: My sister is six months pregnant.
etymology: From embarazar, "to hinder, encumber", probably from Portuguese embaraçar, possibly from baraça, "cord, noose". English embarrass comes from the same source, via French.
fact: One of the most famous false friends in Spanish: an English speaker who means "I'm embarrassed" but says "estoy embarazada" announces a pregnancy.

definition: Expresses a strong wish: "I hope so", "if only". Followed by a verb in the subjunctive.
example: ¡Ojalá que no llueva mañana!
exampleTranslation: Let's hope it doesn't rain tomorrow!
etymology: From Andalusian Arabic law šá lláh, "if God wills", from the centuries of Arabic-speaking rule in medieval Iberia.
fact: Spanish has thousands of words of Arabic origin — many beginning with al-, such as almohada (pillow), aceite (oil) and azúcar (sugar).

definition: Avocado (the fruit or the tree). In parts of South America it's called palta.
example: Corta el aguacate por la mitad y quítale el hueso.
exampleTranslation: Cut the avocado in half and remove the stone.
etymology: From Nahuatl āhuacatl. The Nahuatl word also meant "testicle", most likely because of the fruit's shape.
fact: Guacamole comes from Nahuatl āhuacamōlli, "avocado sauce": āhuacatl + mōlli ("sauce") — the same mōlli as in mole.

definition: Window.
example: Abre la ventana, que hace calor.
exampleTranslation: Open the window — it's hot.
etymology: From Latin ventus ("wind") + the suffix -ana: an opening that lets the wind in.
fact: English window is built on the same idea from a different language: Old Norse vindauga, "wind-eye".

definition: Companion, partner or colleague; compañero de clase is a classmate and compañero de piso a flatmate.
example: Mi compañero de piso cocina muy bien.
exampleTranslation: My flatmate is a very good cook.
etymology: From Vulgar Latin *companio, "one who shares bread": com- ("with") + panis ("bread").
fact: Spanish pan ("bread") keeps the root visible.

definition: Salary or wage; salario mínimo is the minimum wage.
example: Le subieron el salario en enero.
exampleTranslation: They raised his salary in January.
etymology: From Latin salarium, from sal, "salt".
fact: Spanish still has sal for "salt", so the link is easier to see than in English.

gloss: to use or wear for the first time
definition: To use, wear or show something for the first time; also to premiere a film or play.
example: Hoy estreno zapatos.
exampleTranslation: I'm wearing new shoes for the first time today.
etymology: From estrena, "first use; gift", from Latin strena, "omen; a good-luck gift given at the New Year".
fact: English needs a whole phrase for this. The noun estreno means a film or play's premiere.

definition: 1. Lawyer, barrister. 2. Avocado.
example: Mon avocat adore les avocats.
exampleTranslation: My lawyer loves avocados.
etymology: The lawyer sense is from Latin advocatus, "one called to help". The fruit sense came from Spanish aguacate (Nahuatl āhuacatl), reshaped to match the existing word.
fact: Two unrelated words collided into one. English advocate is the lawyer's cousin.

definition: The uncanny feeling of having already experienced the present situation.
example: J'ai une impression de déjà-vu.
exampleTranslation: I have a feeling of déjà vu.
etymology: Literally "already seen": déjà ("already") + vu (past participle of voir, "to see").
fact: The French psychical researcher Émile Boirac is usually credited with popularizing the term in the late 19th and early 20th century.

definition: To wander or stroll without a goal, taking in the surroundings.
example: Le dimanche, on aime flâner le long de la Seine.
exampleTranslation: On Sundays we like to wander along the Seine.
etymology: From Norman French flanner, probably from Old Norse flana, "to wander aimlessly".
fact: The flâneur, an idle observer of city life, became a key figure in 19th-century Paris thanks to writers like Baudelaire.

definition: Friend, pal; mon copain can also mean "my boyfriend" (feminine: copine).
example: Je pars en vacances avec des copains.
exampleTranslation: I'm going on holiday with some friends.
etymology: From Old French compain, the subject form of compagnon, from Late Latin companio, "one who shares bread".
fact: Old French had separate subject and object forms of many nouns. Compain (subject) became copain, and compagnon (object) survived alongside it.

definition: 1. About forty (une quarantaine de personnes). 2. Quarantine. 3. One's forties (il a la quarantaine).
example: Une quarantaine de personnes sont venues.
exampleTranslation: About forty people came.
etymology: From quarante ("forty") + -aine, the suffix for approximate numbers (as in une dizaine, "about ten").
fact: French still uses the everyday "about forty" sense, which shows where the medical meaning came from.

definition: A thick knitted sweater (more common in Quebec; in France, pull is more usual).
example: Mets ton chandail, il fait froid.
exampleTranslation: Put your sweater on, it's cold.
etymology: Shortened from marchand d'ail, "garlic seller". The vendors at the Paris market of Les Halles wore this kind of woollen sweater in the late 19th century.
fact: A rare word built from clipping the middle of a phrase: mar-chand d'ail → chandail.

definition: 1. A wooden clog. 2. An animal's hoof. 3. A wheel clamp (sabot de Denver).
example: Le cheval a perdu un fer à son sabot.
exampleTranslation: The horse lost a shoe from its hoof.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, probably a blend of Old French savate ("old shoe") and bot ("boot").
fact: From sabot came saboter — and English sabotage.

definition: Grapefruit.
example: Je prends un jus de pamplemousse, s'il vous plaît.
exampleTranslation: A grapefruit juice, please.
etymology: From Dutch pompelmoes. Its origin is debated; it's often explained as pompel ("big, swollen") + Portuguese limões ("lemons").
fact: English pomelo — the large citrus fruit that is one of the grapefruit's parents — probably comes from the same Dutch word.

definition: Nursery school for children before primary school, usually ages three to six.
example: Die Kinder gehen morgens in den Kindergarten.
exampleTranslation: The children go to kindergarten in the mornings.
etymology: Kinder ("children") + Garten ("garden"). Named by Friedrich Fröbel in 1840.
fact: German nouns are always capitalized, and their gender has to be learned: der Kindergarten is masculine because der Garten is.

definition: Pleasure derived from someone else's misfortune.
example: Ein bisschen Schadenfreude war dabei, als er im Regen stand.
exampleTranslation: There was a little Schadenfreude when he got caught in the rain.
etymology: Schaden ("harm, damage") + Freude ("joy").
fact: English borrowed the word in the 19th century. Greek had its own word for the feeling: epikhairekakía.

definition: An ache to travel to distant places; the opposite of homesickness.
example: Jedes Mal, wenn ich Flugzeuge sehe, bekomme ich Fernweh.
exampleTranslation: Every time I see planes, I get the urge to travel.
etymology: fern ("far") + Weh ("ache, pain"), modelled on Heimweh ("homesickness").
fact: It is close to Wanderlust, but Wanderlust is the joy of roaming, while Fernweh is closer to an ache for somewhere you are not.

definition: Homesickness; a longing for home.
example: In der ersten Woche hatte sie schlimmes Heimweh.
exampleTranslation: She was terribly homesick the first week.
etymology: Heim ("home") + Weh ("ache, pain"). Originally a Swiss German word.
fact: When Johannes Hofer wanted a learned medical term for Heimweh in 1688, he translated it into Greek and invented nostalgia.

definition: Glove.
example: Ich habe einen Handschuh im Bus verloren.
exampleTranslation: I lost a glove on the bus.
etymology: Literally "hand-shoe": Hand + Schuh ("shoe").
fact: German loves literal compounds: a Stinktier ("stink animal") is a skunk and a Schildkröte ("shield toad") is a turtle.

definition: Window.
example: Mach bitte das Fenster zu.
exampleTranslation: Please close the window.
etymology: Borrowed early from Latin fenestra, "window", when Roman building techniques, including glass windows, spread north.
fact: German took the Latin word and English took the Norse one. English kept fenestra only in learned words like defenestrate.

definition: Poison. (A present is ein Geschenk.)
example: Diese Pilze sind reines Gift.
exampleTranslation: These mushrooms are pure poison.
etymology: From Old High German gift, "something given" — the same origin as English gift. German narrowed it to a "dose" given, and then to poison, much as Greek dósis ("a giving") became English dose.
fact: The old meaning survives in Mitgift, "dowry" — literally what is given along with the bride.

definition: Excess weight put on through comfort eating in times of grief or worry.
example: Nach der Trennung hat er sich etwas Kummerspeck angefuttert.
exampleTranslation: After the break-up he put on a bit of comfort-eating weight.
etymology: Kummer ("grief, sorrow") + Speck ("bacon, fat").
fact: Literally "grief bacon" — a favourite on lists of untranslatable German words.

definition: Disaster, catastrophe; also, informally, a total mess (sei un disastro!).
example: La cucina dopo la festa era un disastro.
exampleTranslation: The kitchen after the party was a disaster.
etymology: From dis- (expressing misfortune) + astro ("star"): an event caused by an unlucky star.
fact: The word spread from Italian to French (désastre) and English in the 16th century, when astrology was taken seriously at European courts.

definition: Forty.
example: Mio padre ha quarant'anni.
exampleTranslation: My father is forty years old.
etymology: From Latin quadraginta, "forty".
fact: Venetian quaranta giorni, "forty days", gave English the word quarantine.

definition: The art of making something difficult look effortless; graceful, practised nonchalance.
example: Suona il piano con una sprezzatura invidiabile.
exampleTranslation: He plays the piano with enviable effortlessness.
etymology: From sprezzare, "to scorn, disdain" (from Latin ex- + pretium, "price, value"): an air of not caring.
fact: Coined by Baldassare Castiglione in The Book of the Courtier (1528) as the essential quality of the ideal Renaissance courtier.

definition: Bankruptcy; fare bancarotta means to go bankrupt.
example: L'azienda ha fatto bancarotta nel 2009.
exampleTranslation: The company went bankrupt in 2009.
etymology: From banca ("bench, counter") + rotta ("broken", from rompere).
fact: Italian banca and banco are the source of English bank — Renaissance Italian bankers really did work at benches in the marketplace.

definition: An informal greeting used both when meeting and when parting.
example: Ciao, ci vediamo domani!
exampleTranslation: Bye, see you tomorrow!
etymology: From Venetian s-ciào, from the phrase s-ciào vostro, "(I am) your slave" — a polite formula of service, from Medieval Latin sclavus.
fact: Austrian and Bavarian German have a greeting with exactly the same logic: Servus, from Latin servus, "servant".

definition: Companion, mate or partner; compagno di classe is a classmate.
example: È il mio compagno di banco da tre anni.
exampleTranslation: He's been my deskmate for three years.
etymology: From Vulgar Latin *companio, "one who shares bread" (com- + panis).
fact: Italian pane ("bread") still sits inside compagnia, "company".

definition: Tomato.
example: Per la salsa servono pomodori maturi.
exampleTranslation: You need ripe tomatoes for the sauce.
etymology: From pomo d'oro, "golden apple". The herbalist Pietro Andrea Mattioli described the new American fruit as pomi d'oro in 1544, possibly because early varieties grown in Europe were yellow.
fact: The Pomodoro productivity technique is named after a tomato-shaped kitchen timer.
